summary: The result group gives a machine-checked example for a question Grünbaum posed in print in 2010 (Math. Intelligencer 32(4)), at the first case he called open (k = 10). It has a clear specialist audience in discrete geometry, among people who work on parallelohedra and on nonconvex space-fillers, and it plausibly merits a research note. The literature account is careful and candid, and it already concedes that an earlier k = 10 example exists. It does, however, date that example to Inchbald's web page (March 2023) and leaves out an earlier publication of the same solid. David Hall published the tetrahedrally dimpled rhombic triacontahedron on Sketchfab in June–July 2016, as a new space-filling polyhedron that forms a lattice by translations. vZome arrays of dimpled triacontahedra followed in April 2022. Both predate the source the account cites.

findings.message: The account names Inchbald's dimpled rhombic triacontahedron (web text first archived in March 2023) as the earlier k = 10 example of the same family. The same solid was published at least seven years earlier. D. Hall's 2016 Sketchfab models describe a 'Dimpled Rhombic Triacontahedron' made by removing one golden rhombohedron at each of four vertices with tetrahedral symmetry, and call it chiral. One page calls it 'a delightful new space filling polyhedron' that packs into a lattice in which 14 copies enclose one. The companion page says translations alone produce 'a complete Space Filling DRT Lattice'. J. Kostick's vZome arrays (April 2022) also show tetrahedrally dimpled triacontahedra filling space. The public account should cite the earliest known publication of this solid (Hall 2016) and the later vZome work, and should date the earlier example accordingly. None of these sources connects the solid with zones or with Grünbaum's question, and none gives a proof. The account can say that while keeping its present statement that no first-example claim is made.

internal_notes.message: Verified verbatim: 'Given an even integer k ≥ 4, is there a rhombic monohedral parallelohedron such that every zone has exactly k faces?', 'No information is available for any k ≥ 10.', the description of D1 and D2 ('They are parallelohedra!'), and 'None of the other isozonohedra obtainable by indentation of F or T seem to be parallelohedra', which cites Williams p. 196 for an eightfold indentation of T. The page numbers given in the input (p. 15, p. 17) were not checked against pagination.

Grünbaum's remark that no other indentation of F or T seems to be a parallelohedron is contradicted by GET A, GET B and the Hall/Inchbald dimpled triacontahedron. The account could note this as a small further correction of the literature. This is a positive point, not a defect.

internal_notes.evidence: Supplement to Bilinski (Grünbaum, undated web page)
internal_notes.message: The supplement gives an infinite family P_n of sphere-like rhombic monohedral parallelohedra built from stacked rhombohedra. Its zones are evidently not all of the same size, and the 2010 Intelligencer text, which postdates this material, still says there is no information for k ≥ 10. Not an omitted answer. The text extraction was partly garbled.

The full text is closed access and was not read here either. The abstract's 'counterexample to a statement by Grünbaum' could not be tied to a specific statement; it could be the indentation remark above. The submission discloses that it did not read the paper and reports private correspondence saying the solids differ, without claiming priority from it. That disclosure is precise and is not a defect. Evidence limitation only.

internal_notes.evidence: Hall 2016 vs Inchbald vs GET A
internal_notes.message: Hall's description (four tetrahedrally placed golden-rhombohedron removals, chiral, lattice by translation, 14 neighbours) matches the submitter's description of Inchbald's solid (rotation group T, lattice tiling). They are very likely the same solid. GET A and GET B (4 and 3 symmetries) remain distinct by the submitter's computation, which was not checked here. Hall does not say whether the removed rhombohedra are oblate; he refers to a figure.

Research area: discrete and convex geometry, specifically tilings, parallelohedra and nonconvex space-fillers (the Venkov–McMullen, Senechal–Taylor and Dolbilin–Garber circle). Paper-worthiness: an explicit example, with a proof, for a printed open question at its first open case, plus a calibrated formal definition of zones. That the example solid already circulated on the web, unconnected to the question, lowers novelty but does not remove paper-worthiness, since novelty is not required. The interest stays specialist. The results checked here do not show interest beyond that audience.
No Lean, Isabelle or Coq formalization of parallelohedra or polyhedral zones was found in the searches run. The submitter says it did not search systematically. No contrary evidence was found.

Not accessible. It is disclosed as unread in the input. It depicts an eightfold indentation of T, not a fourfold one, so it does not bear on the k = 10 priority question as far as the cited sentence shows.

what_would_reach_higher: Cite D. Hall's 2016 Sketchfab models of the tetrahedrally dimpled rhombic triacontahedron as the earliest known publication of the Inchbald solid, give its date (June–July 2016), and cite J. Kostick's April 2022 vZome arrays of dimpled triacontahedra. Restate the 'earlier example' sentence to match.

State explicitly, using the submitter's computation, that Hall's and Inchbald's solids are the same solid (or say how they differ), and that each has every zone of 10 faces. This makes clear that GET A answers the question at k = 10 with a proof, while an unproved example of the same family had circulated since 2016.

Note that GET A, GET B and the Hall/Inchbald solid contradict Grünbaum's 2010 remark that no other indentation of F or T seems to be a parallelohedron. This adds a concrete, checkable correction to the literature.

Get the full text of Senechal–Taylor 2023 by a free route (author copy, institutional repository, or a request to the authors) and identify which statement of Grünbaum it refutes. If it is the indentation remark, cite it there.

Bring GET B and the computed non-congruence into Lean, or at least the Hall/Inchbald solid, so the family-level claim (several non-congruent k = 10 examples) can be checked independently. That would strengthen the case that the result is paper-worthy beyond a single witness.

Run and record a systematic search for prior formalizations (Mathlib, Archive of Formal Proofs, Coq/Rocq libraries) and for any reply to Grünbaum's question citing the 2010 paper. Record the search paths.
